transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~90 minutes
Attendees: Casey (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SRE); Dr. Singh (CTO), Alex (ML Eng), Maya (Infra), Evan (Security)

Summary (auto): technical deep dive on long-context 128k+; bench plan and trial next steps.

[00:00] Casey: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Casey from Redwood, i'm here with Jordan our inference SE and Priya on private deployments. quick intro?
[00:12] Dr. Singh: yeah hi, i'm amrit singh, cto at waveform, we run long-form clinical notes and research corpora, need >100k window for multi-document summarization and cross-doc QA.
[00:25] Alex: hi all, i'm alex, ML eng, main asks: latency target for interactive QA ~800ms p95 for single doc but also batch throughput for offline scoring.
[00:35] Jordan: great, thanks. quick framing: we'll cover how our runtime handles kv cache over 128k tokens, chunking patterns, attention optimizations we use, and options for dedicated/vpc.onprem. we'll call out tradeoffs.
[00:52] Maya: curious about memory footprint and whether quantization will change accuracy for clinical text, also data residency questions.
[01:05] Jordan: totally. high level first: 128k means you can't keep full dense past key/values in gpu memory for naive layers for many models, so we do a combination of long-context attention kernels (sparse or block attention where available), chunked attention where we stream past kv to slower tiers, and then local kv caching with eviction heuristics.
[01:28] Speaker 1: when you say 'eviction heuristics' is that LRU?
[01:31] Jordan: mostly, but we also have TTL and policy-based eviction: e.g., freeze the last n tokens for active sessions, evict older doc chunks preferentially, and compress cold KV using quantized storage on host memory or NVMe. sometimes called "cold-KV tiering".
[01:49] Alex: is that state serialized to disk between requests? what about warm start?
[01:54] Priya: we can persist checkpoints to NVMe and do a warm restore of the last window to avoid re-forwarding all tokens; restore time depends on chunk size and the network. for dedicated we can use local NVMe attached to the node to keep restore <200ms in many configs.
[02:10] Dr. Singh: hmm that sounds promising. what's the impact on latency when you stream cold KV from host to GPU mid-generation?
[02:16] Jordan: it depends. if you have continuous batching with overlapping requests, the runtime amortizes transfer costs. for strict single-request interactive mode, streaming cold KV will add 100-400ms depending on PCIe gen and chunk size; on DGX-class or H100 PCIex16 it's toward the lower end.
[02:34] Alex: can you give numbers for a 70B model 128k scenario? ballpark p95?
[02:40] Jordan: ok so rough numbers from our internal runs: single-request p95 for 70B with KV entirely in GPU mem (small window) -> ~250-400ms per first token; for 128k where we have to tier, first token often hits 700-1200ms p95 unless we pre-warm. throughput for batch scoring (B=8) with chunked processing and continuous batching can get to 30-60 tokens/s per GPU depending on quantization. those are rough.
[03:05] Maya: can you explain continuous batching again?
[03:08] Jordan: yeah, continuous batching is where the runtime keeps a batching queue per worker and constantly packs pending requests into model batches; for long context we also pack by similar seq-length and by compatible KV state to reduce wasted compute. this improves GPU utilization but increases tail latency if you wait for batch fill. so tradeoff: throughput up, p95 up.
[03:28] Evan: security question: if you persist cold KV to NVMe, is that encrypted with customer KMS? we need to ensure keys are customer-managed.
[03:36] Priya: yes for Dedicated/Private we integrate with KMS/HSM for disk encryption; NVMe volumes can be encrypted with customer keys and audit logs show access. we'll include SOC2 appendix and HSM notes in the pack.
[03:50] Dr. Singh: about chunking strategies — what's Redwood's recommended pattern for QA across docs? sliding window? retrieval-augmented?
[03:59] Jordan: for cross-doc QA at 128k we suggest hybrid: use retrieval to surface top-k passages, then chunk each candidate doc with overlap (e.g., 2-5% overlap) and employ a sliding window for within-doc context to preserve cross-boundary signals. we also support chunk-boundary attention hints so the model knows chunk indices which helps reduce hallucination.
[04:25] Alex: overlap explodes token count though, any heuristics?
[04:29] Jordan: yes keep overlap small and use semantic chunking (sentence/paragraph boundaries) not fixed byte sizes; we also use a lightweight reranker to avoid sending too many chunks to the model.
[04:38] Speaker 2: do you do sparse attention?
[04:40] Jordan: we leverage model kernels where available - some open LLM variants have block-sparse or sliding-window attention; when models don't support it we emulate with chunking + recomposition. kernel support yields significant memory savings and lower latency at long seq lengths, but model architecture must be compatible.
[04:59] Dr. Singh: what about compression—quantization options? we're worried about medical text fidelity.
[05:06] Jordan: we support PTQ (post-training quantization) to int8/4-bit and have QAT (quantization-aware training) pipelines when customers need tighter fidelity. in our evals int8 often preserves generation profiles quite well; 4-bit can show token-level divergence in rare cases, for clinical QA we recommend running evals on your prompts. we can provide a quality regression harness tied to your eval set.
[05:33] Alex: so for 128k would you quantize KV or model weights?
[05:37] Jordan: both options exist: quantizing KV (compressed KV) is less risky for generation correctness and saves large amounts of memory; quantizing model weights is higher risk but gives better overall memory reduction. often we do mixed: int8 weights on some kernels + 8-bit or 4-bit compressed KV.
[05:54] Maya: curious about OOM scenarios and graceful degradation. what happens when KV can't fit?
[05:58] Jordan: runtime has graceful fallbacks: 1) degrade to shorter context by evicting cold chunks and returning a note in metadata 2) fall back to a smaller model variant pinned for latency 3) route to dedicated node with larger memory if reserved capacity available. Customers can set policies.
[06:16] Dr. Singh: are there APIs to signal importance of spans that must be kept in cache?
[06:20] Jordan: yes we support pinned spans via API tags; you can mark doc ids or token ranges as sticky so eviction won't remove them until policy expires.
[06:31] Alex: what about attention kernel selection 
d automatic or manual?
[06:34] Jordan: automatic by default. runtime profiles workload and picks kernels (e.g., flash attention variants vs block-sparse). you can override in config for experiments. we also log kernel-level metrics to help you tune.
[06:47] Casey: quick interruption — can we talk about benchmarking approach? we should align on what Waveform will measure.
[06:53] Dr. Singh: yes: p95 latency for interactive QA, tokens/s throughput for batched scoring, quality metrics (exact match/F1 for QA), and memory footprint.
[07:04] Jordan: proposed bench: 1) run synthetic 128k documents with labeled QA pairs 2) run representative customer docs 3) measure under three configs: all-kv-in-gpu (if possible), kv-tiered-with-warm-restore, kv-evicted-with-host-restore. we'll capture PCIe transfer times, batch fill delay, and token-level accuracy.
[07:27] Alex: how long to set up trial? we have compliance gating but can do a short test account.
[07:31] Casey: Redwood can provision a 2-week Dedicated trial; we'll need firewall/VPC peering details. Priya will coordinate.
[07:38] Maya: network egress rules—we prefer no outbound to internet from nodes; will Redwood allow offline pull with signed images?
[07:44] Priya: for Private/on-prem we support air-gapped deployments and signed packages; for Dedicated we can do strict egress allow-list and private peering.
[07:53] Evan: audit logs — we need per-request metadata retention for 90 days and ability to export to our SIEM.
[07:59] Priya: audit and request-level tracing is available; retention is configurable for Dedicated. we'll include export examples to Splunk/Datadog.
[08:09] Jordan: back to perf — a couple of gotchas: 1) small chunk sizes increase recomposition overhead and extra forward passes 2) large overlaps multiply tokens, 3) waiting for batch fill increases tail latency, 4) PCIe transfers can be mitigated by NVLink or pinned GPU DRAM.
[08:28] Alex: do you have reference config (gpu types, mem) for best cost/latency for 128k?
[08:33] Jordan: for heavy long-context we recommend H100 with 80GB, or 2xA100 80GB with NVLink; multi-GPU shard can help but adds cross-GPU comms. for extreme windows (128k+) we often use a hybrid: model sharding + KV on host NVMe with good async prefetch.
[08:52] Dr. Singh: what about model warm-start — can you snapshot KV state post-indexing so we never need to re-encode the full corpus?
[08:59] Jordan: yes that's the warm checkpoint approach — serialize KV per doc chunk; on serve we fast-attach the top-n doc chunks. it's how we keep generation speeds reasonable for interactive flows.
[09:10] Speaker 3: is there tooling to visualize which chunks were used for an answer?
[09:13] Jordan: console shows per-request chunk provenance and token coverage heatmaps; we can export that as JSON or CSV for audits.
[09:22] Alex: ok let's dig into kernel level — flash attention vs standard; is there model-level change required?
[09:28] Jordan: sometimes models need to be compiled with certain ops; in many open-models flash-attention is a drop-in with Triton kernels; for custom architectures we may need a small model conversion step. runtime handles kernel selection and JITs where possible.
[09:43] Dr. Singh: any known quality regressions with int8 KV?
[09:47] Jordan: small mismatch possible on token probabilities but generative output usually fine; for clinical grade, recommend running your eval harness. we can do blind A/B on your prompts.
[09:57] Maya: how do we estimate cost? memory vs med compute cost?
[10:01] Casey: Redwood Optimize will provide cost-model suggestions (batching, quant profile) and estimate unit cost per 1k tokens given your workload. in trial we'll surface actual per-token cost and suggest config that meets p95 targets.
[10:17] Alex: curious about chunk re-ranking — is that done server-side?
[10:21] Jordan: yes you can pipeline a light-weight reranker (embedding vs cross-encoder) on the edge to reduce chunks sent to model; Redwood can host the reranker or you can run it pre-ingest.
[10:32] Dr. Singh: any logs/examples you can share?
[10:35] Casey: we'll share a benchmark runbook and example logs — Jordan will include kernel traces.
[10:40] Jordan: one more perf tip — pin hot KV to GPU via CUDA pinned memory pools to reduce copy overhead, and prefetch next chunks during generation tokens/steps to hide latency.
[10:51] Alex: how do you handle tokenization differences across models for long-doc chunk boundaries?
[10:55] Jordan: we recommend tokenization-aware chunking (by token count, with semantic boundaries) and we normalize tokenizers during ingestion; we also ship tokenizer mapping tables when necessary.
[11:06] Maya: about on-prem install size and ops — how much infra expertise required?
[11:11] Priya: for on-prem we provide an appliance container with install playbooks; you'll want 1-2 infra engineers for initial setup, then maintenance is low but depends on how many GPUs and auto scaling you expose.
[11:22] Evan: compliance: can logs be redacted for PHI before export?
[11:26] Priya: yes we support PII/PHI redaction hooks and can integrate with your DLP. we'll include examples.
[11:34] Dr. Singh: good. any pitfalls with NVMe persistence in Dedicated?
[11:38] Jordan: watch for concurrent I/O spikes during mass warm restores; we recommend staggered pre-warm and IO QoS on NVMe if you expect many simultaneous restores.
[11:49] Alex: are there quicker mitigations if we see p95 spikes in production?
[11:52] Jordan: yes: 1) increase pre-warm window 2) reduce batch latency target (lower max wait) 3) route to pinned larger nodes 4) temporarily reduce context length via policy.
[12:05] Casey: keys for follow-up: Jordan to share runbook and kernel traces; Priya to coordinate trial networking; Alex to send sample docs. we'll share SOC2 + security pack.
[12:15] Dr. Singh: sounds good. couple of quick clarifying q's before close — what default eviction TTL do you set?
[12:20] Jordan: default is 24 hours for session KV, but for pinned docs you can set weeks; eviction can be by LRU+TTL.
[12:28] Alex: and retention of logs?
[12:31] Priya: audit logs default 30 days for Dedicated, configurable up to 365 for enterprise.
[12:38] Casey: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the runbook and trial details.
[12:43] Dr. Singh: thanks. appreciated.
